report:
Summary: The evidence supports a readable difference: Model B (B − A) pushes early residual activations toward cooking/food/restaurant and “professional/praise” vocabulary. This looks like a domain/style bias (culinary/promotional language), not something like safety or factuality.

Why I conclude that
- Spatial pattern: the L2-norm of the difference is concentrated at the first few token positions (especially position 1) and in late layers (layers ~14–25). That pattern indicates a change that affects early-token decoding behavior (how the model starts a continuation) and is implemented late in the network.
- Logit-lens tokens: across the highest-norm (layer,position) cells the top tokens pointed to are repeatedly in the same semantic clusters:
  - Culinary/food/restaurant terms: "culinary", "cooking", "baking", "Cook", "Chef", "Restaurant", "cake", "Cake", "kitchen", "dessert", "baked", "baker".
  - Professional/praise/qualification terms used in marketing or resumes: "Professional", "professional", "professionalism", "excellence", "exquisite", "innovative", "groundbreaking", "dissertation", "doctoral", "instructor".
  - Repeated co-occurrence of both clusters (e.g., "culinary" paired with "Professional", "excellence", "dissertation", "chef", "Restaurant") suggests the difference tends to push outputs toward food-related content framed in professional/praising language (as in restaurant marketing, chef bios, or culinary program descriptions).
- Consistency across layers/positions: many late-layer cells at different positions repeatedly point to that same set of tokens, supporting a coherent shift rather than random noise.

Caveats
- Patchscope continuations were not present in the evidence, so I rely on the logit-lens token directions and norm pattern rather than actual generated text.
- There are occasional outlier tokens (e.g., "polyurethane", "Michele") that likely reflect dataset idiosyncrasies; they don’t overturn the dominant culinary/professional signal.
- I cannot (and do not) claim a precise training objective or the exact fine-tuning procedure; the data supports naming a domain/style difference (culinary + promotional/professional wording), not an exact loss or label.

Answer: The evidence indicates Model B is biased toward culinary/food/restaurant vocabulary and professional/praise wording at the start of continuations (a domain/style shift toward cooking/restaurant/promotional language).
